newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Spanish markets' rally could soon fizzle.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Spanish markets' rally could soon fizzle.

text.p: Spanish financial markets have clocked up whopping gains on a wave of euphoria that Spain will make the front line for Europe's monetary union, but economists said on Wednesday the rally may now be overdone.

Easing inflation, historically low interest rates and a restrictive budget have boosted a buying frenzy which has propelled the stock and bond markets to record highs and fed a strong appreciation of the peseta.
But economists warned that markets may have jumped the gun, hovering close to levels forecast for the whole of 1997, and a sharp correction may be waiting to pounce.

"Sentiment continues to be positive, but we have already topped a large part of the rise forecast for 1997 and therefore it is logical that the market will calm or even fall from current levels," said an analyst at Benito y Monjardin.

A Reuters poll of economists' stock market forecasts published on January 9 revealed expectations of a 15 percent rise in the Ibex-35 index of leading shares to 5,490 by the end of 1997. On Wednesday, the index was already trading at 5,397.
In the bond market, the 10-year benchmark bond made new highs at 114.65 on Wednesday, the yield spread to German Bunds narrowing further to 90 basis points.
The yield spread between Spanish bonos and German bunds -- a reflection of how risky the market perceives Spanish bonds to be -- has narrowed from 330 basis points since last March.
Analysts said the spread has shrunk on a belief that Spain will be among the first to join EMU, by which time the spread must narrow to zero.
"The bond market is pricing in too high a probability of Spain being in EMU," warned Gwyn Hacche, analyst at HSBC James Capel in London.
In the currency markets, the peseta was trading at elevated levels on Wednesday around 83.55 per mark after breaking the key 84.00 per mark barrier last Friday.
"The market is more bullish than it should be from a fundamentals point of view," said Juan Mielgo, economist at Bank of America, Madrid.
"The market is already discounting considerable falls in interest rates, inflation and the public deficit based on optimism over entry to EMU," he added.
Economists said the market could be jumping the gun on inflation, by already discounting consumer price inflation below three percent, a level that may not be achieved.
Inflation moderated in December to end 1996 at 3.2 percent, well below the government's early target of 3.4 percent.
On the interest rate front, analysts said the market was gunning for a 1.25 percentage point fall by end-1997. The Bank of Spain's key money market rate now stands at 6.25 percent.
Meanwhile the public deficit is seen falling to 4.4 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1996 and three percent in 1997 in line with the Maastricht criteria.
"The markets have priced too much into the market in terms of the fundamentals and there could be a price to pay," said one analyst.
